title: Τόξον καὶ χερμάδιον
titleEn: The Bow and the Stone — Iliad 8.292–380
about: Teucer answers Agamemnon's urging: he has shot eight arrows and hit eight men, but cannot hit Hector. He shoots at Hector twice more and misses both times; the first arrow kills Priam's son Gorgythion, the second, turned aside by Apollo, kills Hector's charioteer Archeptolemus. Hector leaps down and strikes Teucer on the collarbone with a stone as he draws his bow; Ajax shields him and two companions carry him to the ships. Zeus then rouses the Trojans again, and Hector drives the Achaeans back through the ditch like a dog on the heels of a boar. Hera sees it and begs Athena to act; Athena complains of Zeus, who forgets how she saved his son Heracles, and goes to arm herself for war.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσεφώνεε Τεῦκρος ἀμύμων·
sentences.l: To him answering spoke Teucer, blameless:
sentences.i: In answer blameless Teucer spoke to him:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσεφώνεε is a reply-formula: τόν ‘him’ is the article used as a pronoun, and the Ἀτρεΐδη of the next line shows that the person answered is Agamemnon. προσεφώνεε is the imperfect of προσφωνέω ‘speak to’, uncontracted (Attic προσεφώνει). ἀμύμων ‘blameless’ is a stock epithet, translated every time; its exact sense is not known, and ‘blameless’ is only the traditional rendering.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη κύδιστε τί με σπεύδοντα καὶ αὐτὸν
ὀτρύνεις;
sentences.l:
“Atreus’-son, most glorious, why me, hastening, even of myself,
do you urge on?
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, most glorious, why do you urge me on, when I am hurrying of my own accord?
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδη is the vocative of the patronymic Ἀτρεΐδης ‘son of Atreus’, here Agamemnon. κύδιστε ‘most glorious’ is the superlative of the adjective from κῦδος ‘glory’. σπεύδοντα ‘hastening’ agrees with με, and καὶ αὐτόν adds ‘even (me) myself’: Teucer is already doing all he can unprompted. ὀτρύνεις is the present of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’.

sentences.t:
οὐ μέν τοι ὅση δύναμίς γε πάρεστι
παύομαι, ἀλλ’ ἐξ οὗ προτὶ Ἴλιον ὠσάμεθ’ αὐτοὺς
ἐκ τοῦ δὴ τόξοισι δεδεγμένος ἄνδρας ἐναίρω.
sentences.l:
Not indeed, you know, as far as strength is at hand
I cease, but from the time when toward Ilios we pushed them back,
from that time on, with bow awaiting them, men I slay.
sentences.i: I do not stop, so far as my strength is at hand; from the time we pushed them back toward Ilios, I have been waiting for them with my bow and killing men.
sentences.n: The unit starts mid-line, with the answer to the question: οὐ … παύομαι ‘I do not cease’, with ὅση δύναμίς γε πάρεστι ‘as far as strength is at hand’ in between. τοι is a particle, ‘you know’. ὠσάμεθ’ is the aorist middle of ὠθέω ‘push’, ‘we pushed them’ (Attic ἐωσάμεθα). δεδεγμένος is the perfect participle of δέχομαι ‘receive, await’, ‘on the watch for’ the men as they come. ἐναίρω ‘slay’ is present, and ἐκ τοῦ ‘from that time’ says it has been going on since.

sentences.t:
ὀκτὼ δὴ προέηκα τανυγλώχινας ὀϊστούς,
πάντες δ’ ἐν χροῒ πῆχθεν ἀρηϊθόων αἰζηῶν·
sentences.l:
Eight indeed I have sent forth long-barbed arrows,
and all in the flesh were fixed of war-swift vigorous young men;
sentences.i: I have shot eight long-barbed arrows, and every one of them stuck fast in the flesh of strong young men, swift in war;
sentences.n: προέηκα is the aorist of προΐημι ‘send forth, let fly’. τανυγλώχινας ‘long-barbed’ joins τανυ- ‘long, stretched’ to γλωχίν ‘barb’ (compare τριγλώχιν ‘three-barbed’). πῆχθεν is the aorist passive of πήγνυμι ‘fix’, with epic -εν for -ησαν. χροῒ is the dative of χρώς ‘skin, flesh’. ἀρηϊθόων is the genitive plural of ἀρηΐθοος, probably ‘swift in war’ (Ἄρης ‘war’ and θοός ‘swift’), though the first part is not certain; αἰζηῶν is from αἰζηός ‘vigorous young man’. The diaeresis in ὀϊστούς and ἀρηϊθόων is as the edition prints it.

sentences.t: τοῦτον δ’ οὐ δύναμαι βαλέειν κύνα λυσσητῆρα.
sentences.l: this one, though, I am not able to strike, this frenzied dog.”
sentences.i: but this one I cannot hit, this frenzied dog.”
sentences.n: τοῦτον … κύνα: Teucer means Hector, whom he does not name. βαλέειν is the epic uncontracted aorist infinitive of βάλλω (Attic βαλεῖν). κύων ‘dog’ is an insult, and λυσσητήρ is built from λύσσα ‘wild frenzy’, so the two words together say ‘frenzied brute’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα καὶ ἄλλον ὀϊστὸν ἀπὸ νευρῆφιν ἴαλλεν
Ἕκτορος ἀντικρύ, βαλέειν δέ ἑ ἵετο θυμός·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and another arrow from the string he sent
straight at Hector, and to strike him his heart was eager;
sentences.i: So he said, and shot another arrow from the string straight at Hector, and his heart was eager to hit him;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα καί ‘he spoke, and’ closes a speech and starts the action. ἴαλλεν is the imperfect of ἰάλλω ‘send, let fly’. νευρῆφιν has the suffix -φι, which here gives the sense ‘from the string’ (νευρή). ἀντικρύ ‘straight at, right opposite’. ἵετο is the imperfect middle of ἵημι, ‘was eager, was set on’, with infinitive βαλέειν; ἑ is the pronoun ‘him’, Hector. θυμός ‘heart’ is the seat of the wish.

sentences.t:
καὶ τοῦ μέν ῥ’ ἀφάμαρθ’, ὃ δ’ ἀμύμονα Γοργυθίωνα
υἱὸν ἐῢν Πριάμοιο κατὰ στῆθος βάλεν ἰῷ,
τόν ῥ’ ἐξ Αἰσύμηθεν ὀπυιομένη τέκε μήτηρ
καλὴ Καστιάνειρα δέμας ἐϊκυῖα θεῇσι.
sentences.l:
and of him indeed he missed, but he blameless Gorgythion,
the good son of Priam, in the chest struck with an arrow,
whom out of Aisyme, being wedded, bore his mother,
fair Castianeira, in form like the goddesses.
sentences.i: and he missed Hector, but he struck blameless Gorgythion, the good son of Priam, in the chest with the arrow, whom his mother, fair Castianeira, bore after she was wedded from Aisyme; in form she was like the goddesses.
sentences.n: The unit starts at line 302 because line 301 ended in the ano teleia. καὶ τοῦ μέν is Hector (‘him indeed he missed’, the genitive after ἀφάμαρθ’, the aorist of ἀφαμαρτάνω ‘miss’), and ὃ δ’ is Teucer, still unnamed. Γοργυθίωνα is the accusative of Γοργυθίων. ἰῷ is the dative of ἰός ‘arrow’. In τόν ῥ’ … τέκε the relative clause explains who Gorgythion is. ὀπυιομένη is the present participle of ὀπυίομαι ‘be taken as wife’, and Αἰσύμηθεν has the suffix -θεν ‘from’ (a place called Aisyme). δέμας ἐϊκυῖα is ‘like in form’, a perfect participle with the accusative of respect; θεῇσι is the epic dative plural of θεά ‘goddess’.

sentences.t:
μήκων δ’ ὡς ἑτέρωσε κάρη βάλεν, ἥ τ’ ἐνὶ κήπῳ
καρπῷ βριθομένη νοτίῃσί τε εἰαρινῇσιν,
ὣς ἑτέρωσ’ ἤμυσε κάρη πήληκι βαρυνθέν.
sentences.l:
And as a poppy to one side its head bends, which in a garden
is weighed down with fruit and with the moist of spring,
so to one side he drooped his head, weighed down by the helmet.
sentences.i: As a poppy bends its head to one side, a poppy in a garden weighed down with its fruit and the damp of spring, so he drooped his head to one side, weighed down by his helmet.
sentences.n: A simile: μήκων ‘poppy’ matched by ὣς … κάρη, ‘so he … his head’. βάλεν in the simile is a general aorist, ‘casts, lets fall’, in the present sense of an English comparison. ἥ τ’ is the relative ‘which’ with the epic τε. καρπῷ ‘fruit’ is the seed-head, and νοτίῃσιν is the dative plural of νοτίη ‘moisture’. ἤμυσε is the aorist of ἀμύω ‘droop, let fall’. βαρυνθέν is a neuter aorist passive participle, because κάρη ‘head’ is a neuter noun; πήληκι is the dative of πήληξ ‘helmet’, the weight that bows Gorgythion’s head.

sentences.t:
Τεῦκρος δ’ ἄλλον ὀϊστὸν ἀπὸ νευρῆφιν ἴαλλεν
Ἕκτορος ἀντικρύ, βαλέειν δέ ἑ ἵετο θυμός.
sentences.l:
And Teucer another arrow from the string sent
straight at Hector, and to strike him his heart was eager.
sentences.i: Teucer shot another arrow from the string straight at Hector, and his heart was eager to hit him.
sentences.n: A repeat of lines 300–301, with Teucer named. The words are the same, so the English is: ἴαλλεν ‘sent’, ἵετο θυμός ‘his heart was eager’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ὅ γε καὶ τόθ’ ἅμαρτε·
sentences.l: but he, even then, missed;
sentences.i: But this time too he missed;
sentences.n: ὅ γε is Teucer. ἅμαρτε is the aorist of ἁμαρτάνω ‘miss’, without the augment. τόθ’ is τότε ‘then’, and καί says that the miss is the second one.

sentences.t: παρέσφηλεν γὰρ Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.l: for threw-off-course Apollo;
sentences.i: for Apollo threw his aim off;
sentences.n: παρέσφηλεν is the aorist of παρασφάλλω ‘make slip aside, throw off the mark’; the object is not stated, and it is Teucer’s shot. γάρ gives the reason for the miss. The god’s hand in the miss is what spares Hector.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ Ἀρχεπτόλεμον θρασὺν Ἕκτορος ἡνιοχῆα
ἱέμενον πόλεμον δὲ βάλε στῆθος παρὰ μαζόν·
sentences.l:
but Archeptolemus, bold, Hector’s charioteer,
rushing to war, he struck in the chest beside the nipple;
sentences.i: but he struck Archeptolemus, Hector’s bold charioteer, as he was rushing into the war, in the chest beside the nipple;
sentences.n: The object comes first: Ἀρχεπτόλεμον … ἡνιοχῆα, accusative, with ἡνιοχῆα the accusative of ἡνιοχεύς, an epic by-form of ἡνίοχος ‘charioteer’. The subject of βάλε (aorist of βάλλω, without the augment) is Teucer, as before. ἱέμενον is the present participle of ἵημι ‘rush’, and πόλεμον δέ is ‘to the war’, with the suffix -δε of direction. θρασύς ‘bold’. ἀλλά, ‘but’, marks the swerve of the arrow from Hector to the man beside him.

sentences.t:
ἤριπε δ’ ἐξ ὀχέων, ὑπερώησαν δέ οἱ ἵπποι
ὠκύποδες·
sentences.l:
And he fell out of the chariot, and swerved aside from him the horses,
swift-footed;
sentences.i: He fell from the chariot, and the swift-footed horses shied away from him;
sentences.n: ἤριπε is the aorist of ἐρείπω ‘fall’ (the η- is the augment). ὑπερώησαν is the aorist of ὑπερωέω ‘swerve, shy aside’; οἱ ‘from him’ is the dative of the dead charioteer. ὠκύποδες ‘swift-footed’ stands in the next line and is the epithet of ἵπποι.

sentences.t: τοῦ δ’ αὖθι λύθη ψυχή τε μένος τε.
sentences.l: and of him on the spot was loosed the soul and the might.
sentences.i: and on the spot his soul and his might were loosed.
sentences.n: τοῦ is the genitive ‘of him’. λύθη is the aorist passive of λύω ‘loose’, in the singular, agreeing with the nearer subject ψυχή; μένος ‘might’ is a second subject. αὖθι is ‘there, on the spot’. This is how the poet says the man died.

sentences.t: Ἕκτορα δ’ αἰνὸν ἄχος πύκασε φρένας ἡνιόχοιο·
sentences.l: And Hector fearsome grief covered about the wits, for his charioteer;
sentences.i: And fearsome grief covered Hector’s wits for his charioteer;
sentences.n: Ἕκτορα is the object of πύκασε (aorist of πυκάζω ‘cover thickly’) together with φρένας, ‘Hector … his wits’; the genitive ἡνιόχοιο gives the cause, ‘for his charioteer’. αἰνόν ‘fearsome’, ἄχος ‘grief’.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἔπειτ’ εἴασε καὶ ἀχνύμενός περ ἑταίρου,
Κεβριόνην δ’ ἐκέλευσεν ἀδελφεὸν ἐγγὺς ἐόντα
ἵππων ἡνί’ ἑλεῖν·
sentences.i: Then he let him be, though he grieved for his companion, and ordered Cebriones, his brother, who was close by, to take the reins of the horses;
sentences.n: τὸν μέν is the dead charioteer. εἴασε, the aorist of ἐάω ‘allow’, has no infinitive after it here and so means ‘let be, left alone’. ἀχνύμενος ‘grieving’, with περ ‘though’, and ἑταίρου is a genitive of cause, ‘for his companion’. Κεβριόνην is the accusative of Κεβριόνης; ἀδελφεόν ‘brother’ (Attic ἀδελφόν) means Hector’s brother. ἐκέλευσεν takes the infinitive ἑλεῖν, the aorist of αἱρέω ‘take’; ἡνί’ is ἡνία ‘reins’, elided.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ οὐκ ἀπίθησεν ἀκούσας.
sentences.l: and he then did not disobey, having heard.
sentences.i: and he did not disobey when he heard.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 319. ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ is ‘and he, then’, the article used as a pronoun for Cebriones. ἀπίθησεν is the aorist of ἀπιθέω ‘disobey’, and οὐκ ἀπίθησεν ‘did not disobey’ is a formula for ready obedience.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δ’ ἐκ δίφροιο χαμαὶ θόρε παμφανόωντος
σμερδαλέα ἰάχων·
sentences.l:
And himself from the chariot to the ground leapt, the all-shining one,
terribly crying out;
sentences.i: and he himself leapt from the shining chariot to the ground, crying out terribly;
sentences.n: αὐτός ‘himself’ is Hector, set against Cebriones. θόρε is the aorist of θρῴσκω ‘leap’, without the augment. παμφανόωντος is the genitive of the participle of παμφανάω ‘shine all over’ (Attic παμφανῶντος), agreeing with δίφροιο ‘chariot’. σμερδαλέα is the neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘terribly’; ἰάχων is the participle of ἰάχω ‘cry out’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ χερμάδιον λάβε χειρί,
βῆ δ’ ἰθὺς Τεύκρου, βαλέειν δέ ἑ θυμὸς ἀνώγει.
sentences.l:
and he a stone took in hand,
and went straight at Teucer, and to strike him his heart urged.
sentences.i: and took a stone in his hand, and went straight at Teucer; his heart urged him on to strike.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 321. λάβε is the aorist of λαμβάνω ‘take’, without the augment, and χερμάδιον is ‘a stone fit to throw’. ἰθύς with a genitive, ἰθὺς Τεύκρου, is ‘straight at Teucer’. βῆ is the aorist of βαίνω ‘go’. ἀνώγει is the imperfect of ἄνωγα ‘urge, bid’.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι ὃ μὲν φαρέτρης ἐξείλετο πικρὸν ὀϊστόν,
θῆκε δ’ ἐπὶ νευρῇ·
sentences.l:
Indeed he from the quiver took out a bitter arrow,
and set it on the string;
sentences.i: He, for his part, took a bitter arrow out of the quiver and set it on the string;
sentences.n: ἤτοι ὃ μέν is ‘indeed he’, Teucer; the edition prints ἤτοι as one word. The ‘but’ that answers it, τὸν δ’ αὖ, is in the next line. ἐξείλετο is the aorist middle of ἐξαιρέω ‘take out’. θῆκε is the aorist of τίθημι ‘set’. πικρόν ‘bitter’ as in πικρὸς ὀϊστός. νευρῇ ‘on the string’ is a dative.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ αὖ κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ
αὐερύοντα παρ’ ὦμον, ὅθι κληῒς ἀποέργει
αὐχένα τε στῆθός τε, μάλιστα δὲ καίριόν ἐστι,
τῇ ῥ’ ἐπὶ οἷ μεμαῶτα βάλεν λίθῳ ὀκριόεντι,
sentences.l:
and him in turn Hector of the glancing helmet,
as he drew back at the shoulder, where the collarbone holds apart
the neck and the chest, and it is the deadliest place,
there, as he was eager against him, struck with a jagged stone,
sentences.i: and as Teucer drew the string back at his shoulder, where the collarbone holds the neck and the chest apart, and where a blow is most deadly, Hector of the glancing helmet struck him there with a jagged stone as he strained against him,
sentences.n: The unit starts in the middle of line 324. τὸν is Teucer, the object of βάλεν (line 327), with αὐερύοντα ‘drawing back’ (the string, left to be understood, the verb being αὐερύω) and μεμαῶτα ‘eager, straining’, both agreeing with it; ἐπὶ οἷ is ‘against him’. κληῒς is the collarbone; ἀποέργει is the present of ἀπείργω ‘hold apart’. καίριον is ‘at the vital spot’, a spot where a wound kills. τῇ ‘there’ picks up ὅθι. ὀκριόεντι ‘jagged’ agrees with λίθῳ. The clause is cut at the comma and the sentence goes on in the next unit.

sentences.t: ῥῆξε δέ οἱ νευρήν·
sentences.l: and broke for him the string;
sentences.i: and broke his bowstring;
sentences.n: ῥῆξε is the aorist of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’, without the augment, and οἱ ‘for him’ is a dative of interest; the subject is understood from the previous unit. The unit is cut at the stop, and the next unit goes on with the effect on the hand.

sentences.t:
νάρκησε δὲ χεὶρ ἐπὶ καρπῷ,
στῆ δὲ γνὺξ ἐριπών, τόξον δέ οἱ ἔκπεσε χειρός.
sentences.l:
and was numbed the hand at the wrist,
and he stood on knee, having dropped, and the bow from him fell out of his hand.
sentences.i: his hand went numb at the wrist, and he dropped on his knee and stayed there, and the bow fell out of his hand.
sentences.n: The unit starts in the middle of line 328. καρπῷ is the wrist (καρπός ‘wrist’, a different word from καρπός ‘fruit’ in line 307). νάρκησε is the aorist of ναρκάω ‘go numb’. στῆ is the aorist of ἵστημι ‘come to a stand’, and γνύξ is an adverb, ‘on the knee’; ἐριπών is the aorist participle of ἐρείπω ‘fall, drop’. ἔκπεσε is the aorist of ἐκπίπτω ‘fall out’, with the genitive χειρός ‘out of the hand’.

sentences.t:
Αἴας δ’ οὐκ ἀμέλησε κασιγνήτοιο πεσόντος,
ἀλλὰ θέων περίβη καί οἱ σάκος ἀμφεκάλυψε.
sentences.l:
And Ajax did not neglect his brother, who had fallen,
but running he strode about and for him the shield enfolded.
sentences.i: But Ajax did not neglect his brother, who had fallen; he ran up, stood over him, and enfolded him with his shield.
sentences.n: κασιγνήτοιο is the genitive of κασίγνητος ‘brother’, with the epic ending -οιο, depending on ἀμέλησε (aorist of ἀμελέω ‘neglect’); οὐκ ἀμέλησε is a negative that says he cared. πεσόντος ‘having fallen’ agrees with it. περίβη, aorist of περιβαίνω ‘step around, bestride’, is the stance of one guarding a fallen man. καί οἱ is ‘and for him’, with ἀμφεκάλυψε the aorist of ἀμφικαλύπτω ‘enfold, cover on all sides’.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἔπειθ’ ὑποδύντε δύω ἐρίηρες ἑταῖροι
Μηκιστεὺς Ἐχίοιο πάϊς καὶ δῖος Ἀλάστωρ
νῆας ἔπι γλαφυρὰς φερέτην βαρέα στενάχοντα.
sentences.l:
Him then, getting under him, two trusty companions,
Mecisteus, Echius’ son, and heavenly Alastor,
to the hollow ships were bearing, heavily groaning.
sentences.i: Then two trusty companions, Mecisteus, son of Echius, and heavenly Alastor, got under him and carried him, groaning heavily, to the hollow ships.
sentences.n: τόν is Teucer. ὑποδύντε is the dual aorist participle of ὑποδύω ‘go under’, to take his weight, and φερέτην is the dual imperfect of φέρω ‘carry’; δύω is ‘two’ (Attic δύο). Both are dual because there are two carriers. ἐρίηρες ἑταῖροι is the stock phrase ‘trusty companions’, and δῖος ‘heavenly’ is the stock epithet. πάϊς ‘son’. νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς is a phrase with the preposition after its noun, ‘to the hollow ships’. βαρέα is an adverb, ‘heavily’; στενάχοντα ‘groaning’ agrees with τόν.

sentences.t: ἂψ δ’ αὖτις Τρώεσσιν Ὀλύμπιος ἐν μένος ὦρσεν·
sentences.l: And back again in the Trojans the Olympian roused might;
sentences.i: Once again the Olympian roused might in the Trojans;
sentences.n: ἂψ … αὖτις is a doubled ‘back again, once more’. ἐν … ὦρσεν is tmesis: the preverb ἐν ‘in’ stands apart from ὦρσεν, the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’ (without the augment), so ‘roused in’ the Trojans. Ὀλύμπιος ‘the Olympian’ is Zeus, left unnamed, and μένος is ‘might’.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἰθὺς τάφροιο βαθείης ὦσαν Ἀχαιούς·
sentences.l: and they straight at the deep ditch pushed the Achaeans;
sentences.i: and they drove the Achaeans straight toward the deep ditch;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ are the Trojans. ἰθὺς τάφροιο is ‘straight at the ditch’, ἰθύς with the genitive as in line 322. ὦσαν is the aorist of ὠθέω ‘push’ (Attic ἔωσαν). βαθείης is the epic feminine of βαθύς ‘deep’.

sentences.t: Ἕκτωρ δ’ ἐν πρώτοισι κίε σθένεϊ βλεμεαίνων.
sentences.l: and Hector among the first went, in his strength exulting.
sentences.i: and Hector went among the foremost, exulting in his strength.
sentences.n: ἐν πρώτοισι ‘among the first’ puts Hector in the front rank. κίε is a past form of κίω ‘go’. σθένεϊ is the dative of σθένος ‘strength’, uncontracted (Attic σθένει), and βλεμεαίνων is the participle of βλεμεαίνω ‘exult, glory’.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτε τίς τε κύων συὸς ἀγρίου ἠὲ λέοντος
ἅπτηται κατόπισθε ποσὶν ταχέεσσι διώκων
ἰσχία τε γλουτούς τε, ἑλισσόμενόν τε δοκεύει,
sentences.l:
And as when some dog a wild boar or a lion
lays hold of from behind, with swift feet pursuing,
the haunches and the buttocks, and watches it as it turns about,
sentences.i: As when a dog, pursuing on swift feet, seizes a wild boar or a lion from behind by the haunches and the buttocks, and watches it as it wheels about,
sentences.n: A simile, begun with ὡς δ’ ὅτε ‘and as when’; the application follows in the next unit. τίς τε is ‘any’ with the epic τε. ἅπτηται is the subjunctive of ἅπτομαι ‘lay hold of’: the animal is in the genitive (συὸς ἀγρίου ἠὲ λέοντος), and the part held is in the accusative (ἰσχία, γλουτούς, ‘haunches’ and ‘buttocks’). κατόπισθε ‘from behind’. ποσὶν ταχέεσσι is an uncontracted dative plural, ‘on swift feet’. ἑλισσόμενον is ‘turning about’, and δοκεύει ‘watches (for)’. The subjunctive has no κεν and no ἄν, as in a simile.

sentences.t:
ὣς Ἕκτωρ ὤπαζε κάρη κομόωντας Ἀχαιούς,
αἰὲν ἀποκτείνων τὸν ὀπίστατον·
sentences.l:
so Hector kept pressing the long-haired-of-head Achaeans,
always killing the hindmost;
sentences.i: so Hector kept pressing the long-haired Achaeans, always killing the hindmost;
sentences.n: ὣς answers the ὡς of the simile. ὤπαζε is the imperfect of ὀπάζω, ‘make follow, press upon’, and the dog’s pursuit of the animal is Hector’s pursuit of the Achaeans. κάρη κομόωντας is the stock phrase ‘long-haired’, literally ‘wearing the hair long on the head’, with the participle uncontracted (Attic κομῶντας). αἰέν is αἰεί ‘always’. ὀπίστατον is the superlative of ὀπίσω ‘behind’, ‘hindmost’, and τὸν ὀπίστατον is ‘whichever was last’.

sentences.t: οἳ δὲ φέβοντο.
sentences.l: and they fled.
sentences.i: and they fled.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 342. οἳ δέ ‘and they’ are the Achaeans. φέβοντο is the imperfect of φέβομαι ‘flee’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ διά τε σκόλοπας καὶ τάφρον ἔβησαν
φεύγοντες, πολλοὶ δὲ δάμεν Τρώων ὑπὸ χερσίν,
sentences.l:
But when through both the stakes and the ditch they had gone,
fleeing, and many were subdued by the hands of the Trojans,
sentences.i: But when they had gone in flight through the stakes and the ditch, and many had been laid low at the hands of the Trojans,
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ‘but when’ opens a clause that waits for its main verb in the next unit (ἐρητύοντο). σκόλοπας ‘stakes’ are the palisade stakes set along the ditch. ἔβησαν is the aorist of βαίνω ‘go’. δάμεν is the aorist passive of δαμάζω ‘subdue, lay low’ (Attic ἐδαμάσθησαν), and Τρώων ὑπὸ χερσίν is ‘under the hands of the Trojans’.

sentences.t:
οἳ μὲν δὴ παρὰ νηυσὶν ἐρητύοντο μένοντες,
ἀλλήλοισί τε κεκλόμενοι καὶ πᾶσι θεοῖσι
χεῖρας ἀνίσχοντες μεγάλ’ εὐχετόωντο ἕκαστος·
sentences.i: these held where they were beside the ships, standing fast, calling on one another and on all the gods, and each man lifted up his hands and prayed loudly;
sentences.n: οἳ μὲν δή ‘these indeed’ sets the Achaeans who got through against Hector, in the next line. ἐρητύοντο is the imperfect passive of ἐρητύω ‘hold back’, ‘were held, stayed put’, and μένοντες ‘remaining’ adds that they stood fast. κεκλόμενοι is the reduplicated aorist participle of κέλομαι ‘call on’. ἀνίσχοντες is ‘holding up’, with χεῖρας ‘hands’. μεγάλ’ is μεγάλα, ‘greatly’, here ‘loudly’; εὐχετόωντο is the uncontracted imperfect of εὐχετάομαι ‘pray’ (Attic εὐχετῶντο).

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δ’ ἀμφιπεριστρώφα καλλίτριχας ἵππους
Γοργοῦς ὄμματ’ ἔχων ἠδὲ βροτολοιγοῦ Ἄρηος.
sentences.l:
while Hector wheeled round about the fair-maned horses,
the Gorgon’s eyes having and those of mortal-ruining Ares.
sentences.i: while Hector wheeled his fair-maned horses about, with the eyes of the Gorgon and of Ares, the ruin of mortals.
sentences.n: ἀμφιπεριστρώφα is the imperfect of a verb with two preverbs, ἀμφιπεριστρωφάω ‘turn round and round’, without the augment (Attic ἀμφιπεριεστρώφα). καλλίτριχας ‘fair-maned’ is the stock epithet of horses. Γοργοῦς ὄμματ’ ἔχων is ‘having the eyes of the Gorgon’: Hector looks as terrible as she does. ἠδέ is ‘and’, and βροτολοιγοῦ ‘mortal-ruining’ is the stock epithet of Ares, in the genitive.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δὲ ἰδοῦσ’ ἐλέησε θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη,
αἶψα δ’ Ἀθηναίην ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
And them seeing, pitied the goddess, white-armed Hera,
and at once to Athena winged words she spoke:
sentences.i: And the goddess, white-armed Hera, pitied them when she saw them, and at once she spoke winged words to Athena:
sentences.n: τοὺς … ἰδοῦσ’ is ‘seeing them’ (the Achaeans), with the aorist participle of ὁράω; ἐλέησε is the aorist of ἐλεέω ‘pity’. θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη is the stock phrase ‘the goddess, white-armed Hera’. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the formula ‘spoke winged words’, with ἔπεα the uncontracted plural of ἔπος and προσηύδα the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι αἰγιόχοιο Διὸς τέκος οὐκέτι νῶϊ
ὀλλυμένων Δαναῶν κεκαδησόμεθ’ ὑστάτιόν περ;
sentences.l:
“Ah, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, no longer we two
for the perishing Danaans shall care, even at the last?
sentences.i: “Ah, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, shall we two no longer care for the Danaans as they perish, even now at the last?
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι is the cry ‘Ah’. αἰγιόχοιο Διὸς τέκος is ‘child of aegis-bearing Zeus’ with the epic genitive -οιο, and Athena is addressed. νῶϊ is the dual ‘we two’. κεκαδησόμεθ’ is the future of κήδομαι ‘care for’, with the genitive ὀλλυμένων Δαναῶν ‘the Danaans as they perish’ (ὀλλυμένων is the present participle of ὄλλυμι). ὑστάτιον is ‘at the last’, with περ ‘even’; the question is Hera’s protest.

sentences.t:
οἵ κεν δὴ κακὸν οἶτον ἀναπλήσαντες ὄλωνται
ἀνδρὸς ἑνὸς ῥιπῇ, ὃ δὲ μαίνεται οὐκέτ’ ἀνεκτῶς
Ἕκτωρ Πριαμίδης, καὶ δὴ κακὰ πολλὰ ἔοργε.
sentences.l:
who indeed, having filled up an evil fate, shall perish
by the onset of one man, and he rages no longer bearably,
Hector, Priam’s-son, and indeed many evils he has done.”
sentences.i: who will fill up an evil fate and perish by the onset of one man; while he rages past bearing, Hector, son of Priam, and he has indeed done many evils.”
sentences.n: The relative οἵ takes up Δαναῶν. κεν with the subjunctive ὄλωνται (aorist of ὄλλυμι) is ‘will, as it may be, perish’, with ἀναπλήσαντες ‘having filled up’ (the aorist participle of ἀναπίμπλημι). ἀνδρὸς ἑνός is ‘of one man’, and ῥιπῇ is ‘onset’, a rush or swing. ἀνεκτῶς is the adverb of ἀνεκτός ‘bearable’, with οὐκέτ’ ‘no longer’. Πριαμίδης is the patronymic ‘son of Priam’. ἔοργε is the perfect of ἔρδω ‘do’, and καὶ δή is ‘and indeed’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.l: Her then in turn addressed the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: Then the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, spoke to her in turn:
sentences.n: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε is a reply-formula, ‘her then in turn addressed’. προσέειπε is the aorist of προσεῖπον ‘speak to’, uncontracted (Attic προσεῖπε). γλαυκῶπις ‘gleaming-eyed’ is the stock epithet of Athena.

sentences.t:
καὶ λίην οὗτός γε μένος θυμόν τ’ ὀλέσειε
χερσὶν ὑπ’ Ἀργείων φθίμενος ἐν πατρίδι γαίῃ·
sentences.l:
“Indeed, quite, may this man at least lose might and life,
perishing under the hands of the Argives in his fatherland, the land;
sentences.i: “May he indeed lose his might and his life, perishing at the hands of the Argives in the land of his fathers;
sentences.n: καὶ λίην is ‘indeed, quite’. ὀλέσειε is the aorist optative of ὀλλύω ‘destroy, lose’, a wish, and οὗτός γε ‘this man at least’ is Hector. μένος ‘might’ and θυμόν ‘life’ are the objects (θυμός is the life that leaves a dying man). φθίμενος is the aorist middle participle of φθίνω ‘perish’. χερσὶν ὑπ’ Ἀργείων is ‘under the hands of the Argives’, and ἐν πατρίδι γαίῃ is ‘in the land of his fathers’, where the adjective is the noun πατρίς ‘fatherland’ and γαίῃ is the dative.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ πατὴρ οὑμὸς φρεσὶ μαίνεται οὐκ ἀγαθῇσι
σχέτλιος, αἰὲν ἀλιτρός, ἐμῶν μενέων ἀπερωεύς·
sentences.l:
but my father in his wits rages, not good ones,
cruel, always sinful, a thwarter of my might;
sentences.i: but my father rages, with wits that are not good, cruel, always sinful, a thwarter of my might;
sentences.n: οὑμός is the crasis of ὁ ἐμός ‘my’. φρεσὶ … οὐκ ἀγαθῇσι is ‘in wits not good’, with the epic dative -ῃσι. σχέτλιος ‘cruel’ is an adjective and ἀλιτρός ‘sinful’ an adjective or noun (‘offender’); both are words of reproach. ἐμῶν μενέων is the genitive plural of μένος ‘might’. ἀπερωεύς is a rare word, and its meaning is not fully known; ‘one who thwarts’ is the usual reading.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τι τῶν μέμνηται, ὅ οἱ μάλα πολλάκις υἱὸν
τειρόμενον σώεσκον ὑπ’ Εὐρυσθῆος ἀέθλων.
sentences.l:
nor of any of it does he remember, which for him very often his son
being worn down I saved from the labours of Eurystheus.
sentences.i: and he remembers nothing of how very often I saved his son when he was being worn down by the labours set by Eurystheus.
sentences.n: οὐδέ τι τῶν μέμνηται is ‘nor does he remember any of those things’, the perfect μέμνηται of μιμνῄσκομαι with the genitive. ὅ is the neuter relative, ‘that, how’, and οἱ ‘for him’ is Zeus. τειρόμενον is the present participle passive of τείρω ‘wear down’, agreeing with υἱόν; the son is not named, but the labours of Eurystheus show it is Heracles. σώεσκον is the iterative imperfect of σώω ‘save’ (-εσκ- ‘used to’), ‘I would save’. ὑπ’ Εὐρυσθῆος ἀέθλων is ‘under the labours of Eurystheus’.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι ὃ μὲν κλαίεσκε πρὸς οὐρανόν, αὐτὰρ ἐμὲ Ζεὺς
τῷ ἐπαλεξήσουσαν ἀπ’ οὐρανόθεν προΐαλλεν.
sentences.l:
Indeed he would weep toward heaven, but me Zeus
to help him would send forth from heaven.
sentences.i: He would weep toward heaven, but Zeus would send me down from heaven to help him.
sentences.n: κλαίεσκε is the iterative imperfect of κλαίω ‘weep’, ‘he would weep’, set against ἐμέ ‘me’ in the next clause. The ὃ μέν is the son. ἐπαλεξήσουσαν is the future participle of ἐπαλέξω ‘come to the aid of’, feminine, agreeing with ἐμέ, and τῷ ‘him’ is its dative. προΐαλλεν is the imperfect of προϊάλλω ‘send forth’. οὐρανόθεν has the suffix -θεν ‘from’.

sentences.t:
εἰ γὰρ ἐγὼ τάδε ᾔδε’ ἐνὶ φρεσὶ πευκαλίμῃσιν
εὖτέ μιν εἰς Ἀΐδαο πυλάρταο προὔπεμψεν
ἐξ Ἐρέβευς ἄξοντα κύνα στυγεροῦ Ἀΐδαο,
οὐκ ἂν ὑπεξέφυγε Στυγὸς ὕδατος αἰπὰ ῥέεθρα.
sentences.l:
For if I had known this in my keen wits,
when him to Hades the gate-fastener he sent forth,
to bring out of Erebus the dog of hateful Hades,
not would he have escaped the steep streams of the water of the Styx.
sentences.i: If I had known this in my keen wits, when he sent him forth to Hades, the gate-fastener, to bring the dog of hateful Hades out of Erebus, he would not have escaped the steep streams of the water of the Styx.
sentences.n: εἰ γάρ with the past tense ᾔδε’ (the pluperfect of οἶδα, ‘I had known’) and the aorist with ἄν in οὐκ ἂν ὑπεξέφυγε make a condition that was not met: she did not know. The subject of προὔπεμψεν (προ- and ἔπεμψεν run together) is not stated; it is Eurystheus, from the labours of line 363, and μιν is Heracles. εἰς Ἀΐδαο has no noun: ‘to (the house of) Hades’. πυλάρταο is a rare epithet whose sense is not fully known, usually taken as ‘gate-fastener’. πευκαλίμῃσι ‘keen’ is also not fully known. ἄξοντα is the future participle of ἄγω ‘lead’, ‘to bring’, and κύνα ‘dog’ is Cerberus, unnamed. Ἐρέβευς is the genitive of Ἔρεβος. ὑπεξέφυγε is the aorist of ὑπεκφεύγω ‘escape from under’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἐμὲ μὲν στυγέει, Θέτιδος δ’ ἐξήνυσε βουλάς,
ἥ οἱ γούνατ’ ἔκυσσε καὶ ἔλλαβε χειρὶ γενείου,
λισσομένη τιμῆσαι Ἀχιλλῆα πτολίπορθον.
sentences.l:
But now me he hates, and of Thetis he has fulfilled the plans,
who his knees kissed and took hold with her hand of his chin,
begging him to honour Achilles the city-sacking.
sentences.i: But now he hates me, and has carried out the plans of Thetis, who kissed his knees and took hold of his chin with her hand, begging him to honour Achilles, the city-sacker.
sentences.n: νῦν δ’ ‘but now’ turns from the past to the present. στυγέει is the uncontracted present of στυγέω ‘hate’. ἐξήνυσε is the aorist of ἐξανύω ‘accomplish’, and βουλάς is ‘plans’. In ἥ οἱ … the relative ἥ is Thetis and οἱ is ‘his’ (Zeus’s). γούνατ’ is γούνατα ‘knees’, and ἔλλαβε χειρὶ γενείου is ‘took hold with her hand of the chin’, with the genitive of the part touched: touching knees and chin is the gesture of a suppliant. λισσομένη ‘begging’ goes with τιμῆσαι ‘to honour’. πτολίπορθος ‘city-sacker’ is a stock epithet of Achilles.

sentences.t: ἔσται μὰν ὅτ’ ἂν αὖτε φίλην γλαυκώπιδα εἴπῃ.
sentences.l: There will be a time, indeed, when again his dear gleaming-eyed one he calls.
sentences.i: There will indeed be a time when he again calls me his dear gleaming-eyed one.
sentences.n: ἔσται μάν is ‘there will indeed be (a time)’, and ὅτ’ ἂν … εἴπῃ is ‘when he may call’, the aorist subjunctive of λέγω ‘speak of, call’ with ἄν. αὖτε is ‘again’. φίλην γλαυκώπιδα is ‘his dear gleaming-eyed one’, a pet name made from the epithet γλαυκῶπις; the speaker is Athena, so the person called by it is herself, though ἐμέ is not said.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὺ μὲν νῦν νῶϊν ἐπέντυε μώνυχας ἵππους,
ὄφρ’ ἂν ἐγὼ καταδῦσα Διὸς δόμον αἰγιόχοιο
τεύχεσιν ἐς πόλεμον θωρήξομαι,
sentences.l:
But you now for us two make ready the solid-hoofed horses,
until I, having gone down into the house of aegis-bearing Zeus,
with armour for war arm myself,
sentences.i: But you, for now, make ready the solid-hoofed horses for the two of us, until I have gone into the house of aegis-bearing Zeus and armed myself with armour for war,
sentences.n: ἐπέντυε is the imperative of ἐπεντύω ‘make ready, harness’, and νῶϊν is the dual dative ‘for us two’. μώνυχας ἵππους is the stock phrase ‘solid-hoofed horses’. ὄφρ’ ἂν … θωρήξομαι is ‘until I arm myself’, the aorist subjunctive of θωρήσσω ‘arm’ with an -ο- ending. καταδῦσα is the aorist participle of καταδύω ‘go down into’, and τεύχεσιν is ‘with armour’, a dative plural. The clause runs on in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὄφρα ἴδωμαι
ἢ νῶϊ Πριάμοιο πάϊς κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ
γηθήσει προφανέντε ἀνὰ πτολέμοιο γεφύρας,
sentences.l:
so that I may see
whether at us two, Priam’s son, Hector of the glancing helmet,
will rejoice, when we appear along the bridges of war,
sentences.i: so that I may see whether Priam’s son, Hector of the glancing helmet, will be glad when the two of us appear along the bridges of war,
sentences.n: ὄφρα ἴδωμαι is a purpose clause, the aorist subjunctive of ὁράω; it starts in the middle of line 376. ἢ … ἦ τις sets two things in front of her: ‘whether Hector will rejoice … or whether some Trojan will …’. The ἦ of the second is Attic ἤ ‘or’. πάϊς ‘son’, κορυθαίολος ‘of the glancing helmet’, the stock epithet of Hector. γηθήσει is the future of γηθέω ‘rejoice’, and προφανέντε is a dual aorist passive participle, and νῶϊ (dual, not the dative νῶϊν of line 374) goes with it: Hector will be glad at ‘us two having appeared’. What the πτολέμοιο γεφύρας ‘bridges of war’ are is not known; it seems to mean the open ground in the fighting.

sentences.t:
ἦ τις καὶ Τρώων κορέει κύνας ἠδ’ οἰωνοὺς
δημῷ καὶ σάρκεσσι, πεσὼν ἐπὶ νηυσὶν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l:
or whether some one even of the Trojans will sate dogs and birds
with fat and with flesh, having fallen by the ships of the Achaeans.”
sentences.i: or whether one of the Trojans, fallen by the ships of the Achaeans, will glut dogs and birds with his fat and flesh.”
sentences.n: ἦ τις καί goes with the ἢ of the line before: ‘or whether some one even of the Trojans’. κορέει is the uncontracted future of κορέννυμι ‘sate’ (Attic κορεῖ), with κύνας ἠδ’ οἰωνούς ‘dogs and birds’ as its object. δημῷ ‘fat’ and σάρκεσσι ‘with flesh’ are datives, the second with the epic ending -εσσι. πεσών is the aorist participle of πίπτω ‘fall’. The speech ends here, as Athena goes to arm.
